section.title: Abram and Lot Part
section.sectionRationale: Restored to the land after Egypt, Abram faces a new test: strife over land forces him to part from Lot. The unit runs from the return, through the generous parting and Lot's fateful choice, to God's renewal of the promise, and it holds together as a study in faith that lets go and trusts God to provide.
section.thesis: Abram trusts the promise enough to give Lot first choice of the land, and though Lot grasps the best for himself, God confirms to open-handed Abram the whole land and a countless offspring.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the return from Egypt and the strife between herdsmen; Abram's generous offer and Lot's choice toward Sodom; and the LORD's renewal of the land and offspring promise.

units.label: Back in the land, and strife

verses.text: So Abram went up out of Egypt into the Negev, he and his wife and all his possessions, and Lot was with him.
And Abram had become extremely wealthy in livestock and silver and gold.
From the Negev he journeyed from place to place toward Bethel, until he came to the place between Bethel and Ai where his tent had formerly been pitched,
to the site where he had built the altar. And there Abram called on the name of the LORD.
Now Lot, who was traveling with Abram, also had flocks and herds and tents.
But the land was unable to support both of them while they stayed together, for they had so many possessions that they were unable to coexist.
And there was discord between the herdsmen of Abram and the herdsmen of Lot. At that time the Canaanites and the Perizzites were also living in the land.
So Abram said to Lot, “Please let there be no {{riv|contention}} between you and me, or between your herdsmen and my herdsmen. After all, we are kinsmen.
Is not the whole land before you? Now separate yourself from me. If you go to the left, I will go to the right; if you go to the right, I will go to the left.”

And Lot looked out and saw that the whole plain of the Jordan, all the way to Zoar, was well watered like the garden of the LORD, like the land of Egypt. (This was before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah.)
So Lot {{bachar|chose}} the whole plain of the Jordan for himself and set out toward the east. And Abram and Lot parted company.
Abram lived in the land of Canaan, but Lot settled in the cities of the plain and pitched his tent toward Sodom.
But the men of Sodom were wicked, sinning greatly against the LORD.
After Lot had departed, the LORD said to Abram, “Now lift up your eyes from the place where you are, and look to the north and south and east and west,
for all the land that you see, I will give to you and your offspring forever.
I will make your {{zera|offspring}} like the dust of the earth, so that if one could count the dust of the earth, then your offspring could be counted.
Get up and walk around the land, through its length and breadth, for I will give it to you.”
So Abram moved his tent and went to live near the Oaks of Mamre at Hebron, where he built an altar to the LORD.

riv.gloss: Strife, quarrel, or contention. The same root names the place Meribah, where Israel later quarrels with God. Here Abram acts to prevent strife within the family, choosing peace over his own rights as the elder and the one to whom the land was promised.

bachar.gloss: To choose or select. Lot chooses for himself the well watered plain, walking by sight toward Sodom. His self-serving choice contrasts sharply with Abram's faith, and it will lead him step by step into the orbit of a doomed and wicked city.

zera.gloss: Seed or offspring. God promises Abram a seed as countless as the dust of the earth, echoing the promise of Genesis 12 and reaching forward to Christ and to all who are Abram's children by faith, Galatians 3:29.

basic.context: Abram comes back from Egypt very rich, and so is his nephew Lot. Their flocks are so large that the land cannot hold them both, and their herdsmen start quarrelling. To keep peace in the family, Abram offers Lot first pick of the land.
basic.hermeneutics: The key question is why Abram, the elder with the promise, gives up his right to choose first. The answer is faith: Abram trusts God to provide, so he can afford to be generous. Lot, by contrast, chooses by what looks best and drifts toward wicked Sodom.
basic.originalLanguages: Abram acts to stop the strife, a word linked to Israel's later quarrelling with God. Lot chooses the good-looking plain for himself, walking by sight. And God promises Abram an offspring, a seed, as countless as the dust, the same word that runs all the way to Christ.
basic.typology: Abram's giving up his rights for the sake of peace points to the way of Christ, who did not grasp but gave. The countless offspring promised here is fulfilled in Jesus and the great family of faith. And Lot pitching his tent toward Sodom warns of the pull of the world.
basic.christ: Abram lets go of the best land and trusts God, and God gives him everything; this is the pattern Jesus lived and taught, that the one who loses his life will find it. The promised seed as numberless as the dust is finally gathered in Christ, in whom people from every nation become Abram's children.
basic.god: God rewards faith with reassurance. The moment Lot leaves, God speaks, confirming to open-handed Abram the whole land and a countless family. He is generous to those who trust Him and lets go, and He is the God who keeps renewing His promises.
basic.crossReferences: Jesus teaches that the meek inherit the earth and that losing your life for His sake is the way to save it. Paul says all who belong to Christ are Abram's offspring. And Hebrews notes Abram lived as a pilgrim, waiting for a better country.
basic.oneStory: Abram trusts the promise enough to hold his rights loosely and let Lot grab the best. God answers by pledging him the whole land and a countless seed. This is the way of faith that runs through the Bible to Jesus, who gave up everything and so inherited all things, and who makes a countless family from every nation.

context.literary:
Genesis 13 closes a loop that opened in Genesis 12:8. There Abram pitched his tent between Bethel and Ai, built an altar and called on the name of the LORD. Then came the famine, the descent into Egypt and the lie about Sarai. Verses 3 and 4 bring him back to the very spot, 'where his tent had formerly been pitched,' 'the site where he had built the altar,' and he calls on the name of the LORD again. The detour to Egypt is bracketed and closed, and the story resumes at the altar where it paused.

The chapter itself is framed by altars. It opens with worship at Bethel, verse 4, and closes with a new altar at Hebron, verse 18. Between them lie three movements: a problem, verses 5 to 7; a choice, verses 8 to 13; and a promise, verses 14 to 17.

The hinge is a repeated phrase that English translations often smooth over. In verse 10 Lot literally 'lifted up his eyes' and saw; in verse 14 the LORD tells Abram, 'lift up your eyes.' The same gesture opens two scenes. Lot looks for himself and chooses; Abram looks at God's bidding and receives. Lot's view runs east toward one well watered plain; Abram's runs to all four points of the compass.

The narrator also slows the story with a parenthesis in verse 10, 'This was before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah,' and a comment in verse 13 on the men of Sodom. Both reach forward to chapters 18 and 19. Lot's movement is traced in stages, choosing the plain, settling in its cities, pitching his tent toward Sodom, and by Genesis 14:12 he is 'living in Sodom' and by Genesis 19:1 sitting in its gateway. The drift is told in verbs. Lot also sets out 'toward the east,' verse 11, the direction the early chapters associate with leaving God's presence, Genesis 3:24, 4:16 and 11:2.
context.historical:
Abram and Lot were pastoralists moving flocks and herds between seasonal grazing grounds in the central hill country. For such men the limits of a region were set by water and pasture, and verse 6 states the problem in those terms: the land 'was unable to support both of them.' Quarrels between rival herdsmen over wells and grazing were the ordinary friction of that life; Genesis records the same kind of dispute again in Genesis 21:25 and 26:20.

The wealth that caused the crowding came partly from Egypt. Pharaoh had given Abram sheep, cattle, donkeys, servants and camels, Genesis 12:16, and verse 2 adds silver and gold. Israel, reading this, would remember that they too came up out of Egypt carrying silver and gold, Exodus 12:35-36.

From the ridge near Bethel a man can see east down into the Jordan valley. The 'plain of the Jordan,' literally the circle or round of the Jordan, was the fertile basin around the lower river and the southern end of the Dead Sea. Genesis compares it to 'the garden of the LORD' and to Egypt, the two best watered places the first readers knew. Zoar, verse 10, sat at its southern edge. The region's later desolation was well known to Israel, which is why the narrator must explain that the view Lot saw came 'before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah.'

The note that 'the Canaanites and the Perizzites were also living in the land,' verse 7, is more than scenery. Two families of foreigners quarrelling in front of the settled peoples was both dangerous and a poor witness, and it underlines that Abram owned none of the land he was promised. Mamre near Hebron, where he settles in verse 18, became his long term home; he would later buy a burial cave there, Genesis 23:19, and Hebron would be where David was first anointed king, 2 Samuel 2:4.
context.canonical:
The promise of verses 14 to 17 is the second statement of the land promise, enlarging Genesis 12:7. There God said, 'I will give this land to your offspring'; here the gift includes Abram himself, extends 'forever,' and adds the image of offspring like the dust. The images keep growing: stars in Genesis 15:5, and stars and sand together in Genesis 22:17. The dust image is passed to Jacob in almost the same words, 'Your descendants will be like the dust of the earth, and you will spread out to the west and east and north and south,' Genesis 28:14, and Balaam, looking down on Israel's camp, asks, 'Who can count the dust of Jacob?' Numbers 23:10.

The command to look in every direction echoes at the end of the Pentateuch. Moses stands on Nebo and the LORD shows him the whole land, as far as Zoar, and says, 'I have let you see it with your own eyes,' Deuteronomy 34:1-4. The command to walk the land is taken up in the promise to Joshua, 'every place where the sole of your foot will tread,' Joshua 1:3, compare Deuteronomy 11:24.

The garden comparison of verse 10 returns in the prophets. Isaiah 51:3 promises that God will make Zion's desert 'like the garden of the LORD,' and Joel 2:3 describes a land like Eden turned to wasteland, the very reversal that befell Lot's plain.

The New Testament uses both men. Galatians 3:16 draws on this promise, which the BSB notes at verse 15, to argue that the seed is ultimately One. Romans 4:13 widens the land to the world: Abraham would be 'heir of the world.' Hebrews 11:9 remembers him living in tents in the land of promise. Lot is called 'a righteous man' in 2 Peter 2:7-8, tormented by what he saw and heard, and Jesus makes the days of Lot a warning about His return, Luke 17:28-32.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses sets two responses to the same situation side by side so that Israel would see what faith looks like when property is at stake. Abram had just shown, in Egypt, what fear looks like: grasping for safety by a lie, Genesis 12:11-13. Back at the altar he acts differently. He does not appeal to his seniority or to the promise, though both were on his side. He names the relationship first, 'we are kinsmen,' and lets the younger man choose. That is faith doing its work in the most ordinary place, a dispute over grazing.

The author also wants his hearers to notice how Lot's choice is made. Every detail comes through the eyes: he looked, he saw, it was well watered, it was like Egypt. Nothing is said about the LORD, about the altar just behind him, or about the character of Sodom's men. Israel, about to enter a land full of attractive cities and fertile valleys, was being taught to ask more than whether a place looked good.

Finally, the chapter is meant to show that God's speech follows Abram's surrender. The LORD speaks 'after Lot had departed,' verse 14, and gives in every direction what Abram had offered in one. The first hearers were to learn that the promise is not protected by clutching it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter is narrative, and it does not lay down a rule for dividing property or settling family disputes. Abram's particular method, offering the other party first choice, is not commanded, and Scripture elsewhere allows for just claims and fair settlements. What the passage commends is the disposition behind the method: a readiness to lose for the sake of peace because God is trusted to provide. The New Testament asks the same of believers in other words, 'Why not rather be wronged?' 1 Corinthians 6:7, and 'live at peace with everyone,' Romans 12:18.

Lot's choice is also described rather than legislated. The text does not forbid living near cities or choosing good land. It warns against choosing by sight alone, without reference to God or to moral danger. Believers apply it by asking what a decision will do to their souls and their households, not only what it will add to their holdings, Luke 12:15.

debates.question: Was Lot's choice merely unwise, or morally culpable?

views.label: Understandable but spiritually reckless
views.case: The narrator frames the choice with ominous notes, the parenthesis about Sodom's destruction in verse 10 and the verdict on its men in verse 13, and traces Lot's drift from the plain to the cities to Sodom itself, Genesis 14:12 and 19:1. The choice is made by sight alone, with no reference to God, and it leads step by step into danger.

views.label: A reasonable decision with tragic consequences
views.case: Abram offered the choice freely, and taking good grazing land for large herds was a sensible thing for a herdsman to do. Nothing in verse 11 condemns Lot outright, and 2 Peter 2:7-8 calls him 'a righteous man' who was distressed by Sodom's conduct. On this reading the tragedy lies in where he later settled, not in the choice itself.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree that the text holds Lot's choice up against Abram's. Even a lawful choice can be made for the wrong reasons, and the story shows how a decision governed only by what looks profitable can lead, one step at a time, to a place a person would never have chosen at the start.

debates.question: Is the land promised 'forever' in verse 15 fulfilled in the land of Canaan, or in something larger?

views.label: A literal and ongoing promise of Canaan to Abraham's physical descendants
views.case: The promise names a visible territory Abram could see and walk, verses 14 and 17. Later texts treat it as an oath still in force, Psalm 105:8-11 and Genesis 17:8, and some readers expect a future national fulfilment in the land itself.

views.label: A promise that widens to the whole renewed creation in Christ
views.case: Paul calls Abraham 'heir of the world,' Romans 4:13, and Hebrews says the patriarchs were looking for 'a better country, a heavenly one,' Hebrews 11:16. Jesus promises that the meek 'will inherit the earth,' Matthew 5:5, widening Psalm 37:11. On this view Canaan was the first installment and picture of a world restored.

debates.bearing: Whatever one concludes about the land of Israel, the New Testament plainly does not shrink the promise; it enlarges it. Abram himself never owned more than a burial plot, Acts 7:5, and yet he died believing. The promise was always bigger than the ground he stood on.

study.originalLanguages:
The quarrel is named twice with two related words. Verse 7 reports a riv between the herdsmen, a dispute or contention, the word later used for a legal case. In verse 8 Abram pleads, 'let there be no merivah,' a noun from the same root. That second form is the word that gives its name to Meribah, where Israel 'quarreled with the LORD,' Exodus 17:7 and Numbers 20:13. Abram moves to stop between brothers the kind of strife his descendants would later bring against God Himself.

Abram's reason, 'we are kinsmen,' is literally 'we are men, brothers,' anashim achim. The word ach covers a wide range of kin; Lot was his nephew, Genesis 11:31, but Abram chooses the closest word available. The appeal rests on belonging, not on rank.

Verse 10 uses a fixed idiom, nasa einayim, to lift up the eyes. The BSB renders it 'Lot looked out,' but the Hebrew matches verse 14 exactly, where God says, 'lift up your eyes.' The phrase is common in Genesis and often marks a decisive look, as when Abraham lifts his eyes and sees the ram, Genesis 22:13. The sequence in verses 10 and 11 is saw, it was good and well watered, he chose. That pattern of seeing and taking recalls Genesis 3:6 and Genesis 6:2, where the sons of God 'saw' and took 'whomever they chose,' using the same verb bachar. In most of the Old Testament bachar is the verb of God's electing choice, Deuteronomy 7:6; here a man chooses 'for himself.'

The 'plain of the Jordan' is kikkar hayarden. Kikkar means something round: a round loaf, a disk shaped talent of metal, and so a circular basin of land. Genesis 19:29 calls the destroyed towns 'the cities of the plain' with the same word.

Verse 13 piles up its verdict: the men of Sodom were ra'im, evil, and chatta'im, sinners, 'against the LORD,' with the intensifier me'od, greatly. The phrase 'against the LORD' puts the offence first in relation to God, not only to neighbours, as Ezekiel 16:49-50 also does when it lists Sodom's arrogance and neglect of the poor.

Finally, verse 17 says 'walk around the land' with hithallekh, the reflexive stem of the verb to walk, meaning to walk to and fro or go about freely. The same stem describes God walking in the garden, Genesis 3:8, and Enoch walking with God, Genesis 5:22. Abram is to move through the land as one at home in it. And the dust of verse 16, afar, is the same word as the dust from which the man was formed, Genesis 2:7, and to which he returns, Genesis 3:19. The stuff of mortality becomes the measure of blessing.

typology.type: Abram yielding his rights for the sake of peace
typology.fulfillment: Abram held the promise and the senior place, yet gave both up in practice for the sake of peace, and God then gave him more than he surrendered. Christ shows the pattern in full: existing in the form of God, He 'did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied Himself,' and 'therefore God exalted Him,' Philippians 2:6-9. The escalation is vast. Abram gave up first choice of pasture; Christ gave up the glory of heaven and His own life. Abram's generosity also sat beside real failures, as in Egypt, whereas Christ's self emptying was perfect and without mixed motives.

typology.type: Offspring like the dust of the earth, verse 16
typology.fulfillment: The promise sets a number no one could count against a man with no child. It began to be kept in Israel, 'Who can count the dust of Jacob?' Numbers 23:10, but the New Testament finds its full measure in the family gathered in Christ: 'if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham's seed,' Galatians 3:29, a multitude 'too large to count, from every nation,' Revelation 7:9. The type points beyond itself because physical descent could never make a people from every nation; only union with the one Seed, Galatians 3:16, could do that.

typology.type: Abram walking the length and breadth of the land, verse 17
typology.fulfillment: Abram was told to walk through a land he did not own, taking hold of it by faith before possession. Joshua's generation would receive 'every place where the sole of your foot will tread,' Joshua 1:3, but even that conquest did not complete the promise, Hebrews 4:8. Paul says Abraham's heirs inherit 'the world,' Romans 4:13, and Jesus says the meek 'will inherit the earth,' Matthew 5:5. Believers now walk through a world that is theirs in Christ, 1 Corinthians 3:21-23, though they do not yet possess it. The type falls short of the reality, since Canaan was a strip of land and the promise is a new creation.

typology.type: Lot choosing the well watered plain toward Sodom
typology.fulfillment: Lot's choice is a negative pattern, a picture of choosing by sight what looks like Eden and proves to be under judgment. Jesus draws on it directly: 'It was the same in the days of Lot,' with people buying and planting until the day fire fell, Luke 17:28-32. Paul contrasts that way of life with the believer's: 'we walk by faith, not by sight,' 2 Corinthians 5:7. Unlike the other types here, this one does not point to Christ by likeness but warns of the world He calls His people out of, and Lot's rescue, Genesis 19:29, shows mercy even to the one who chose badly.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first by pattern. Abram, holding the promise, releases his claim and lets another choose; God then gives him the whole land. Jesus taught this as a law of the kingdom: 'whoever loses his life for My sake will find it,' Matthew 16:25. He also lived it. Philippians 2:6-9 describes the Son who 'did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied Himself,' and 'therefore God exalted Him to the highest place.' Abram's small surrender over grazing land is a faint outline of that great one. Where Abram's openness sprang from trust that God would provide, Christ's sprang from perfect trust in the Father and perfect love for those He served.

It leads to Christ by promise. Verse 15 promises the land 'to you and your offspring forever,' and the BSB notes that Paul cites it. In Galatians 3:16 Paul argues that the promise was spoken 'to your seed,' meaning One, who is Christ. The countless offspring of verse 16 and the single Seed are not in tension; the many become Abraham's children by belonging to the One, Galatians 3:29.

It leads to Christ by the widening of the inheritance. Abram was told to look north, south, east and west. Jesus promises the meek that they 'will inherit the earth,' Matthew 5:5, and Paul can tell believers 'All things are yours,' 'and you belong to Christ,' 1 Corinthians 3:21-23. The one who grasped nothing becomes the heir of all things, Hebrews 1:2, and those in Him share the inheritance.

It leads to Christ by contrast in Lot. Lot saw a plain 'like the garden of the LORD' and chose it, and it turned out to be under sentence. Jesus warns that the world will look settled and prosperous right up to the day of judgment, 'It will be just like that on the day the Son of Man is revealed,' Luke 17:30. He calls His people to seek first the kingdom of God, Matthew 6:33, and trust that the rest will be added.

The reading must stay modest. Abram is not a sinless figure of Christ; one chapter earlier he lied to save his skin. The link lies in the shape of faith that God honours, a shape that only Christ fills completely, and in the promise itself, which God keeps in Him.
study.god:
The first thing the chapter shows about God is that He restores. Abram returns from a failure in Egypt, where God protected Sarai despite Abram's lie, and he comes back to 'the site where he had built the altar,' verse 4. God has not moved and has not withdrawn the promise. The worship Abram offers there is received, and the story picks up where it left off. God's faithfulness is not the reward of Abram's faithfulness; it precedes it and carries it.

The chapter shows God as the true Owner of the land. Canaanites and Perizzites live in it, verse 7, and Lot takes the best of it, yet God speaks as the One who has every direction at His disposal: 'all the land that you see, I will give to you.' The gift is not diminished by what Lot took. That shapes the doctrine of God's sovereignty in a practical way. God's purposes are not at the mercy of other people's choices, even choices that seem to take the best portion.

God's timing is also telling. He speaks 'after Lot had departed,' verse 14. There is no word from God when Abram makes the offer, none when Lot chooses. God lets the test run its course. Then, when Abram stands with what looks like the smaller share, God speaks. He is the God who meets people in the place of loss with a larger word.

He is also the God who judges. Verse 13 records His verdict on Sodom before any judgment falls, and the parenthesis of verse 10 announces the outcome ahead of time. He sees wickedness 'against the LORD' and does not overlook it, as Genesis 18 and 19 will show. Yet the same God rescues Lot, 'He remembered Abraham,' Genesis 19:29. His justice and His mercy work in the same story.

For worship, the chapter's frame is instructive. It begins and ends at altars, verses 4 and 18. Between them is a family quarrel, a costly decision, a bad choice by another and a promise renewed. The right response to a God who gives this way is the one Abram makes: move the tent, build an altar, call on His name.

crossReferences.note: The first land promise and the first altar between Bethel and Ai. Genesis 13:3-4 brings Abram back to exactly this place after Egypt, and 13:14-17 enlarges this promise, adding Abram himself, the word forever, and the image of dust. Reading them together shows the promise growing, not shrinking, after failure.

The woman saw that the tree was good and pleasing to the eyes, and took. Lot's choice in 13:10-11 follows the same order, seeing what is well watered and choosing it for himself, with the telling comparison to the garden of the LORD. The echo invites readers to see a second fall in miniature.

God repeats the dust promise to Jacob almost word for word, adding that he will spread out west, east, north and south, the same four directions Abram was told to survey in 13:14. The promise passes intact to the next generations, confirming it rested on God, not on Abram.

Moses on Nebo is shown the whole land, as far as Zoar, and told, 'I have let you see it with your own eyes.' Like Abram, he sees what he will not personally possess. Both scenes teach that the land is received as a promise before it is held as property.

When the cities of the plain are destroyed, God remembers Abraham and brings Lot out. The plain Lot chose in 13:10-11 is the place of catastrophe, yet Lot is spared for the sake of the man who gave up his choice. Abram's generosity is repaid in mercy to the one who took the best.

Peter calls Lot 'a righteous man' who was 'tormented in his righteous soul by the lawless deeds he saw and heard.' This balances Genesis 13. Lot's choice drew him into a city that grieved him; he was not at home there, yet he stayed. The warning is aimed at believers, not only at the wicked.

Jesus uses the days of Lot to describe the world before His return, with eating, buying, planting and building up to the day fire fell. The well watered plain of Genesis 13:10 becomes the picture of a prosperous world under judgment, and 'Remember Lot's wife' presses the warning home.

Christ did not grasp at what was His by right but emptied Himself, and God exalted Him. Abram's yielding of first choice in Genesis 13:8-9, followed by God's promise of everything in 13:14-17, is a small outline of the same pattern of humility followed by exaltation.

The BSB notes that Paul cites Genesis 13:15. He argues that 'to your seed' is singular and points to Christ. The promise of land to Abram and his offspring forever finds its heir in one Person, and through Him in all who belong to Him, Galatians 3:29.

Paul says the promise was that Abraham 'would be heir of the world,' and that it came through the righteousness of faith. The land Abram surveyed in Genesis 13:14-15 is widened to the world, and the way to inherit it is faith, not law or grasping.

Abraham lived in the promised land 'as a stranger,' in tents, looking for 'the city with foundations, whose architect and builder is God.' Genesis 13:18 ends with Abram moving his tent again. Even at Hebron he held the land by promise, with his eyes on something God would build.

Jesus declares that the meek will inherit the earth, taking up Psalm 37:11. Abram, who let Lot choose and did not press his claim, receives the promise of all the land. The meek are not the losers in God's economy; they are the heirs.

study.oneStory:
The first chapters of Genesis are a story of people reaching for what God had not given them: the woman seeing and taking in Genesis 3:6, the sons of God seeing and taking in Genesis 6:2, the builders of Babel reaching for a name in Genesis 11:4. Each grasp moved humanity further east, away from God. Genesis 12 begins a new line. God calls one man and promises to give him a land, a name and a seed, so that through him the blessing lost in Eden might reach all the families of the earth, Genesis 12:3.

Genesis 13 tests whether that man will live by grasping or by receiving. Lot repeats the old pattern: he lifts his eyes, sees a plain like Eden, chooses it for himself and heads east. Abram does the opposite. He lets go, and God gives. For the first time in Genesis a man is offered the best portion and declines to take it by force, and God answers with the widest promise yet.

The chapter sets up much of what follows. Lot's choice leads into the war of Genesis 14, the intercession of Genesis 18 and the fire of Genesis 19. Abram's promise grows into the covenant of Genesis 15 and 17. His descendants will later stand where he stood, looking over the same land from Nebo, Deuteronomy 34:1-4, and walking it under Joshua. Yet even the conquest does not finish the story. Israel, like Lot, is repeatedly drawn to what looks good and loses the land in exile.

The promise comes to rest in Christ, the Seed to whom the land was pledged, Galatians 3:16, who did not grasp but emptied Himself and was given the name above every name, Philippians 2:9. In Him the dust like family is gathered from every nation, and the inheritance is widened from Canaan to the world, Romans 4:13.

In the new creation the meek inherit the earth, Matthew 5:5, and the city Abraham waited for comes down from God, Hebrews 11:10. The land he walked as a stranger becomes the home of a people who will never need to move their tents again.

quiz.q: Why did Abram let Lot choose first?

options.text: He trusted God to provide, so he could hold his rights loosely and seek peace.
options.note: Abram's generosity flows from faith in God's promise.

options.text: He was afraid of Lot and gave in to avoid a fight.
options.note: It was faith and peace-making, not fear, that moved Abram.

options.text: God had commanded him to give Lot the best land.
options.note: God gave no such command; Abram chose to be generous.

options.text: As the elder, he wanted to keep peace in the family.
options.note: True, and the deeper root was his faith that God would still provide.

quiz.q: What guided Lot's choice of the Jordan plain?

options.text: What looked best to the eye, drawing him toward Sodom.
options.note: Lot walked by sight, and the text notes Sodom's wickedness.

options.text: A word from God directing him there.
options.note: God spoke to Abram, not to Lot, about the land.

options.text: A desire to protect Abram from danger.
options.note: Lot chose for himself, not out of concern for Abram.

options.text: The good grazing the well watered land offered.
options.note: True on the surface, but the deeper issue was choosing by sight toward a wicked city.

quiz.q: What did God do right after Lot departed?

options.text: He confirmed to Abram the whole land and a countless offspring.
options.note: God rewarded Abram's faith by renewing the promise.

options.text: He rebuked Abram for giving up the best land.
options.note: God did not rebuke him; He reassured and blessed him.

options.text: He immediately destroyed Sodom.
options.note: Sodom's judgment comes later, in chapter 19.

options.text: He told Abram to look in every direction at the land He would give.
options.note: True; part of the renewed promise, which also included countless offspring.

quiz.q: How does Abram's example point to Jesus?

options.text: He held his rights loosely and trusted God, the way Christ did not grasp but gave.
options.note: Abram foreshadows the self-giving way of Christ.

options.text: He seized the best for himself as Jesus did.
options.note: Neither grasped; both gave, which is the point.

options.text: He built a great city like the one Jesus builds.
options.note: Abram built altars and lived as a pilgrim; the link is faith, not city-building.

options.text: He chose peace over conflict, as Christ makes peace.
options.note: True and good, though the sharpest link is holding possessions loosely in trust.

quiz.q: What is the promise of offspring like the dust of the earth about?

options.text: A countless family, fulfilled in Christ and all who are Abram's by faith.
options.note: The seed promise runs to Christ and the worldwide family of faith.

options.text: Only the physical nation of Israel and no one else.
options.note: Israel is included, but the New Testament widens it to all who believe.

options.text: A promise that quietly failed since Abram was still childless.
options.note: The promise did not fail; God fulfilled it in time and ultimately in Christ.

options.text: A reference to Abram's growing wealth in livestock.
options.note: It speaks of descendants, not livestock or riches.

questions: Abram could be generous because he trusted God to provide. Where would trusting God free you to hold your possessions or rights more loosely?
Lot chose by what looked best and drifted toward trouble. Where are you tempted to make big decisions by appearances rather than by faith?
Abram sought peace with a relative rather than winning the argument. Is there a family tension where you could choose peace over your rights?
God reassured Abram right after he let go. When have you found that surrendering something to God was met by His provision?
Jesus said the one who loses his life will find it. What is one thing you sense God asking you to release in order to follow Him more freely?

translationNotes.note: The plain is described as like the garden of the LORD and like Egypt, echoing Eden and Abram's recent detour; the parenthesis before the LORD destroyed Sodom warns the reader that this beauty is doomed.
The Oaks, or Terebinths, of Mamre near Hebron become a settled base for Abram; the note that he built an altar marks worship as the anchor of his life in the land.
